prompt: A page on `https://evil.example` runs `fetch("https://bank.example/transfer", {method: "POST", body: "to=x"})`. The bank sends no CORS headers. Assume no CSP or other sending restriction and a reachable server. What does CORS itself do?

options.text: The browser refuses to send the request at all
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. A `POST` with a form-style body is a simple request, so it is sent without any preflight. The SOP blocks reading the response, not sending it.

options.text: The simple request can be sent, but the script cannot read the response without CORS permission
options.explanation: Correct. This simple request needs no preflight. The server may accept or reject it; absent CORS permission the response is not exposed. Default fetch credentials mode omits cross-origin cookies.

options.text: The request is sent, and the script can read the response because it was a POST
options.explanation: The method does not grant read access. Only a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header does.

options.text: The server rejects it automatically because the Origin header is foreign
options.explanation: Servers do nothing with `Origin` unless their code checks it. The SOP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

workedExample: The string body gives a safelisted text/plain content type, and this POST has no unsafe author-set headers. Under the stated assumptions the browser sends it without preflight, but default cross-origin fetch does not include bank cookies. The server decides whether any action is authorised. Without allow-origin permission the CORS fetch rejects; it does not expose response contents. CSRF still matters for requests that carry eligible ambient credentials or otherwise cause an unauthorised action.

options.text: It lets a server tell browsers which other origins may read its responses, relaxing the same-origin policy
options.explanation: Correct. CORS is a relaxation the server chooses to grant: the server grants read access to named origins via response headers.

options.text: It protects an API from requests made by scripts on other sites
options.explanation: CORS is not a server-side firewall. Simple requests are still delivered, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely.

options.text: It encrypts cross-origin traffic between browser and server
options.explanation: Encryption is TLS's job. CORS is just a set of HTTP headers that control browser read access.

options.text: It stops a page from embedding cross-origin images and scripts
options.explanation: Classic no-cors embedding may work, but CORS-enabled images, module scripts and other resource modes can require CORS approval. Embedding also depends on CSP, CORP/COEP and framing policy.

workedExample: CORS grants browser response-sharing permission and controls preflight approval for non-safelisted requests. Simple requests can still be sent without permission to read the response, while failed required preflights can prevent the actual request. Non-browser clients are not bound by browser CORS enforcement. The server must authenticate and authorise independently.

prompt: A SPA makes CORS fetches to another origin, with no cached preflight permission. Assume safelisted header values where named, no extra author-set headers, no streaming body or upload-listener trigger, and no other sending restriction. Which need an OPTIONS preflight? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: GET with safelisted headers is a simple request; no preflight.
Correct. `application/json` is not one of the three safelisted content types, so it needs a preflight.
Correct under the supplied empty-cache conditions. DELETE is not a CORS-safelisted method.
Correct. `Authorization` is not a CORS-safelisted header, so even a GET is preflighted.
`multipart/form-data` is safelisted (an HTML form can send it), so this is a simple request.

workedExample: Under these assumptions, GET with a safelisted Accept value and POST with a safelisted multipart content type avoid preflight. JSON content type, DELETE and the Authorization header require permission and therefore OPTIONS with an empty preflight cache. Header lengths/bytes and API-specific flags matter too; a header name alone is not the complete safelist test.
